newsitem.title: UK: UK Labour eyes reform of monetary policy-making.
newsitem.headline: UK Labour eyes reform of monetary policy-making.

text.p: Britain's opposition Labour party, in an important reform of economic policy-making procedures, is planning to set up a Council of Economic Advisers that would give guidance to the Chancellor of the Exchequer on the formulation of monetary policy.

Aides to Gordon Brown, Labour's economics spokesman, said the council would replace the so-called panel of independent forecasters, created to advise the chancellor in the wake of sterling's ejection from the European Exchange Rate mechanism in September 1992.

Brown, whose party is hot favourite to win Britain's looming election, will make the commitment in a keynote speech on Wednesday (1800 GMT) in which he will also pledge to follow a tough inflation target.

Labour officials declined to specify the target, but in the past they have said it would be no less tough than the Conservative government's goal of reducing inflation to 2.5 percent or below -- the lower end of a range of one-four percent.
Brown agreed the makeup of the new CEA -- the name is consciously copied from the White House Council of Economic Advisers -- during private talks with the Bank of England.
The panel will comprise the governor of the central bank, his deputy , two Bank of England executive directors and three or four outside figures.
Brown acknowledges the usefulness of the outside advice that the panel independent forecasters has been able to give Chancellor of the Exchequer Kenneth Clarke, the current finance minister.

But aides said Brown had concluded that the present arrangements were too haphazard and that the monthly meetings between Clarke and BoE governor Eddie George to set interest rates had become too personalised and at times too confrontational.
Under present arrangements, the governor of the central bank must do the chancellor's bidding on interest rates.

Labour has shied away from promising to make the Bank of England independent but has said it would give it more operational autonomy to hit the government's inflation target if it succeeded in establishing a successful track record for its advice -- hence the importance of the new CEA.

Financial markets will pay close attention to Brown's speech to see whether he broadens the new council's remit to include the goal of supporting economic growth alongside the containment of inflation, a move that would invite comparison with the U.S. central bank, the Federal Reserve.

The inflation record of past Labour governments is not enviable, but Brown will say that Labour under moderate leader Tony Blair hates inflation because it hits hardest the poor and those on fixed incomes.
"Inflation undermines business success. It creates instability and it harms investment," Brown will say.

Brown's speech is intended to slot into place the last pieces of the macroeconomic jigsaw that he has assembled recently, notable with a commitment to adopt the Conservative's spending plans for the next two years and to freeze income tax rates for the five-year life of the next parliament if Labour wins power.
